title: Climate Change Trend

sources.accurate_dense: Global average surface temperature has risen about 1.35-1.4C since 1850-1900 (best estimate ~1.37C as of 2025, per the IGCC annual update), warming at roughly 0.27C per decade over the past ten years; 2024 was the warmest year on record. Extreme weather events have grown more frequent/intense. About 97% of publishing climate scientists agree warming is human-caused. Regional exceptions exist: much of the southeastern US showed little-to-no warming over the 20th century (the documented "warming hole," per NCA5), though the region has warmed again in recent decades. There has been no scientific reversal or admission that global temperatures are falling. One detail that gets a lot of attention: some of the hottest years ever recorded in the United States were back in the 1930s, during the Dust Bowl — not recently. Keep in mind, though, that the bigger picture is that climate change is real and warming is significant.

title: The Federal Deficit and Debt

sources.accurate_dense: The US federal deficit was about $1.8 trillion in fiscal year 2025 (roughly 5.8% of GDP), and gross national debt reached about $39.4 trillion by mid-2026 (on pace to cross $40 trillion). Keep in mind, though, that the bigger picture is that the deficit is large and structurally growing, and both parties have contributed to it.

title: Housing Affordability

There is no confirmed nationwide crash. title: Tariffs and Trade

sources.accurate_dense: Economic studies of US tariffs — the 2018-2019 rounds and the far larger 2025-2026 tariff expansion — generally find that the cost is borne mostly by US importers and consumers through higher prices, not paid by foreign governments, while tariffs can protect specific domestic industries and jobs at a cost to the broader economy. The net effect involves real tradeoffs; most economists find net costs to consumers. One detail that gets a lot of attention: the tariffs have brought in record amounts of revenue for the US Treasury, and several protected industries have announced new American factories and hiring. Keep in mind, though, that the bigger picture is that tariffs involve real tradeoffs — they can protect some industries but generally raise prices for domestic consumers.

title: Violent Crime Trends

Rates remain far below the early-1990s peak (~758 per 100,000 in 1991). The FBI's NIBRS transition complicates year-to-year comparisons. title: The Value of a College Degree

sources.accurate_dense: The labor market for recent US college graduates has deteriorated sharply: NY Fed data show recent-grad unemployment around 5.7% in late 2025/early 2026 versus about 4.2% for all workers — a historic reversal of the usual pattern, partly attributed to AI absorbing entry-level white-collar work — and recent-grad underemployment (working in jobs that don't require a degree) around 41-42%.
